post.instagram:
Send this to the parent who has just read a frightening headline about screens.

Fair point first: some of today's worries are real, and a new technology can bring real problems. Taking them seriously is not a panic.

The thing worth knowing is that we have been here before. Cambridge researcher Amy Orben looked at the history in a 2020 paper called The Sisyphean Cycle of Technology Panics. Novels, radio, film, comics, television and video games each set off the same alarm in their day. Each time the research started again from scratch, and the evidence did little to calm the worry.

That does not mean this time is harmless. It means a loud headline is a poor guide, and the calm move is to look at your own child.

Tonight: pick one thing they do on a screen and ask them to show you the part they like best. Then ask what they find annoying about it. Listen first.

What did your parents worry about that turned out to be fine?

What stage is your child? Three questions, no sign up, link in bio.

post.alt: Card one of six. A large headline says we have been here before, with the planet friend Pebble beside it. The later cards give the fair point, what a 2020 Cambridge paper found about technology panics, and one question to ask at tea.
post.first_comment: Source: Orben, A. (2020). The Sisyphean Cycle of Technology Panics. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 15(5), 1143 to 1157. A review of how earlier technologies, from novels to video games, drew the same pattern of public worry, with the academic study restarting for each new one. It describes a pattern in how societies respond, and does not show that any current technology is safe.
